title: Haakon VII ready to take on task of succeeding Harald V - EFE - Agencia de noticias
content: ​Oslo, Aug 29 (EFE).- King Haakon VIII expressed his readiness on Saturday to take on and make his mark on the great task of succeeding the late monarch, his father, Harald V. He also thanked the public for all their expressions of affection in his first address to the Norwegian nation as king. ​“Now that my father has passed away, there is a big task ahead of me. He constantly reminded us in the family that everyone must do things their own way. Find their own form. Be themselves. He succeeded his father King Olav, who in turn succeeded his father King Haakon,” he said. ​He expressed gratitude for the tremendous support of his wife, Queen Mette-Marit, and his children. King Haakon also thanked his mother, Queen Sonja, and his sister, Marta Luisa, for the strength they are giving him despite being in mourning. He emphasized that his family has learned how important it is to stay united to be strong, even in difficult times, and added that this unity provides great strength for the important task he must carry out for Norway. ​Haakon VIII, 53, has embraced, just as his father and his father’s father did, the motto “Alt for Norge” (Everything for Norway). ​He recalled that King Harald guided the country through a time of great change, while acknowledging that the world has become more uncertain and unpredictable than it was during most of his father’s reign. ​He highlighted the role of his mother, Queen Sonja, who helped them form a strong royal couple that complemented each other perfectly, he said, noting that this Saturday marks the 58th anniversary of their wedding. ​“Congratulations on your wedding anniversary, dear mother,” he said. ​Haakon also expressed gratitude for the Norwegian people’s expressions of support and solidarity. ​“We are in mourning. At the same time, it gives us comfort and strength that so many people are grieving with us. It has been a powerful and moving experience to see the Palace Square filled with people, flowers, greetings and lights. Thank you very much,” he added. ​Harald V died on Friday at the Kingdom Hospital in Oslo, where he had been admitted on Aug. 17. ​Harald V had been hospitalized due to anemia, but his condition worsened when his illness led to a blood infection, and by Thursday his condition was very serious. The coffin of the late monarch arrived at the Royal Palace on Friday well past 7:00 pm local time, having been transported from the Kingdom Hospital, amid the anticipation of the crowd along the route to witness the hearse’s passage in the relentless rain. title: Queen marks wedding date as Norway mourns King Harald V - Yahoo
content:
Norway's Queen Sonja marked her 58th wedding anniversary alone on Saturday, a day after the death of her husband, King Harald V. The king died on Friday at the age of 89 after spending nearly two weeks in hospital. Queen Sonja, also 89, now faces life without the partner with whom she shared decades of marriage. Their relationship was a love story that overcame considerable opposition. Sonja Haraldsen, then a commoner, first met the Norwegian prince as a teenager. She encountered him again at the age of 22 and the two fell instantly in love. However, Harald's father, then king Olav, strongly opposed their relationship, forcing the couple to keep it secret for nine years. In the end, Harald threatened his father that he would remain unmarried if he was not allowed to be with Sonja. Olav relented, and on August 29, 1968, the couple married at Oslo Cathedral. Crown prince Haakon was born five years later. Following his father's death, he has been King Haakon VIII since Friday. The new king addressed the nation in an emotional televised speech on Saturday evening. "Thank you for being such a good dad to Märtha and me," Haakon said on Saturday evening in a speech broadcast on Norwegian television and radio. With Harald's death, Haakon immediately became the new monarch of the Scandinavian country. He has one sister, Princess Märtha Louise. "You were also a warm and funny grandfather. A loving and caring husband. A generous father-in-law," the king continued. "You supported and took care of us all." "I will miss him," the 53-year-old said of his father. "I will miss his laugh" and his warm, cheerful way of approaching people and situations. His voice briefly faltered as he turned to his mother and said: "Happy wedding anniversary, dear Mum." Looking ahead to his own reign, Haakon said he intended to follow his father's example while finding his own way as monarch. Books of condolence were made available across Norway, allowing members of the public to leave messages of sympathy and remembrance. In Oslo, Mayor Anne Lindboe was among the first to leave a personal message for the monarch, according to the newspaper VG. "You didn't need a crown to be king," she wrote, according to the report. Sweden's Crown Princess Victoria also paid tribute to the late king -- her godfather -- with moving words. "King Harald was a dearly loved godfather - always warm and kind-hearted," she wrote in a statement. "He had a contagious laugh and always a twinkle in his eye." The Norwegian monarch had been "an exceptionally wonderful person" and a role model. "Some people leave a mark that time can never erase. King Harald was one such person," Victoria continued. Memorial services are due to be held on Sunday in numerous churches and in all 11 of Norway's cathedrals. A service at Oslo Cathedral is scheduled to begin at 11 am (0900 GMT), the Church of Norway said. "We mourn the loss of King Harald and feel deep, sincere gratitude for everything he has meant to us all through his life and work," says Olav Fykse Tveit, the presiding bishop of the Church of Norway. Members of the public who wish to pay their respects in person will be able to visit the palace chapel in the coming days. After a brief period in the palace's Red Salon, the king's closed coffin will lie in state in the chapel on a draped platform at specified times until the burial. No date has yet been announced for his funeral, which will be held as a state funeral and is expected to be a major national memorial service. According to the NTB news agency, the ceremony is set to begin in the castle chapel, attended only by the king's closest family members. The king's coffin will then be carried in a funeral procession to Oslo Cathedral. This will be followed by a further funeral procession - on a much smaller scale - to the king's final resting place in Akershus Church. The daily VG newspaper reported that the day of the funeral will not be an official public holiday. However, employees and all school pupils are to be allowed to watch the funeral service. There will be a nationwide minute's silence at 1 pm. title: Argentina v Australia: Five takeaways as 'warrior' and 'brilliant double-act' help continue 'purple patch' under Les Kiss - Planet Rugby
content: Carter Gordon and Josh Canham impress for the Wallabies against Argentina. Following a 27-21 triumph for Australia over Argentina at Estadio 23 de Agosto in San Salvador de Jujuy, here’s our five takeaways from the clash on Saturday. Australia ran out thoroughly deserved winners in this absorbing fixture as they grabbed four tries to Los Pumas’ three and dominated most facets of play in the match. Three tries inside the opening quarter of the game set them on their way as Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Carter Gordon and Fraser McReight all crossed before Tom Hooper was their only try scorer in the second 40. Ryan Lonergan added seven points off the tee before he was replaced due to injury after another impressive outing at the base. Geronimo Prisciantelli and Joaquin Moro scored for Argentina in the opening half and Boris Wenger crossed for the other try, with Santiago Carreras converting all three. But as mentioned, this was a richly earned victory for the Wallabies, who continue their purple patch in this period of transition, with all the signs looking very positive. This is four wins in a row for the Wallabies as the baton that has been handed from Joe Schmidt to Les Kiss has gone swimmingly thus far. There’s a lot to like about them too. Some of the rugby on show from Australia was wonderful as they mixed real steel up front with a slick attacking game that caused Los Pumas problems again and again. Springboks v All Blacks: Five takeaways as Rassie Erasmus’ tinkering pays off as South Africa rediscover their power game to level the series As mentioned, this run of wins dates back to Schmidt’s last match in charge against Italy and Kiss has carried it on with two wins over Japan and this versus Argentina. If they can back this up against Los Pumas in a week’s time it would do the men in gold’s confidence the power of good before they take on South Africa on September 27. Lining up alongside each other for the first time since July 18, Josh Canham and Jeremy Williams quickly settled into their work and starred in the engine room today. Canham’s and Williams’ efforts with ball in hand in the lead-up to Paenga-Amosa’s score on seven minutes was the stuff of outside backs and they would continue to earn their corn around the field thereafter, finishing on 29 and 31 metres respectively in a brilliant double-act at the coalface for Australia that will delight head coach Kiss. Williams almost got a try for his efforts in the closing stages but was adjudged to have been just short of the line. After his hearty showing it felt harsh to chalk it off. In contrast, it is now just one victory in five for Argentina and what makes this all the more concerning is that all of those matches have been played on their home patch. All Blacks player ratings: Breakout star ‘mammoth’ and Will Jordan ‘classy’ but Ruben Love has ‘first real struggle’ Defeats to Scotland, England and South Africa have now been followed by Australia getting one over them and deservedly so it must be said as the Wallabies were on song. The pressure must be mounting on Felipe Contepomi and they simply have to bounce back next week as their usual home fortress appears to be crumbling around them. They desperately need to end this two-Test series on a positive or it will be a gloomy break from action before they resume the Nations Championship later this year. Back-to-back starts at fly-half for Gordon and he is better for it, of that there is no doubt. The 25-year-old was a real warrior today, like many of his teammates, but it was his ability to find gaps and attack the space in Argentina’s defence that really caught the eye as he formed a good combination with Lonergan and later Tate McDermott. There’s no question there’s a greater steel to the Wallabies of late, especially up front, but the backline too were rock solid as Gordon and Max Jorgenson especially never took a backward step and were crucial contributors in this away victory. Surely Kiss has to stick with the returning rugby league convert for the rematch next weekend? title: Harald V, King Of Norway And Former Olympian, Dead At 89 - Yahoo
content:
Europe lost both its oldest monarch and a former Olympian on Saturday as King Harald V of Norway passed away. He was 89 years old. King Harald passed away early Friday morning and his son was subsequently coronated as King Haakon VIII, who announced his father's passing in his first address to the nation as their new king. Harald has reigned since January 1991 following the passing of his father, Olav V. "Yesterday morning at 6:35, His Majesty King Harald V, my father, whom I loved so dearly, passed away. We are grieving. At the same time, it brings us comfort and strength to know that so many are grieving with us. It has been a powerful and moving experience to see the Palace Square filled with people, flowers, messages and candles. Thank you so much," King Haakon said in his address. Decades before he ascended to the throne of Norway though, Harald had been a passionate sports sailor and represented his country in the 1964, 1968 and 1972 Olympics in various sailing competitions. Though he never medaled at the Olympics, his sailing crew went on to enjoy championship success during the 1980s, winning a World Championship in 1987 and silver and bronze medals in 1982 and 1988 respectively. Even after ascending to king, Harald remained a passionate competitive sailor, participating in the 2007 World Championship at the age of 70 and finishing sixth in the competition. Harald served as Norway's flagbearer in the 1964 Olympics in Tokyo and helped organized the 1994 Winter Olympics in his nation's city of Lillehammer. title: Owner Takes His Cadillac Escalade-V to a Tuner, Goes Home With an Extra 200 Horsepower - autoevolution
content:
It has already become a pattern for the owner of this Cadillac. The same tuner, based in the Houston, Texas, area, has built him a couple of cars, including the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing Le Monstre Edition, before he shipped his brand-new Cadillac Escalade-V to them as well. It’s obvious that he doesn't do stock. Standard just doesn’t cut it for him. When it rolls off the production line of the Arlington Assembly plant in Arlington, Texas, the 6.2-liter V8 with supercharged firepower pumps out 682 horsepower (691 metric horsepower) and 653 pound-feet (885 Newton meters) of torque at the crank. That V8 pushes the 6,352-pound (2,881-kilogram) behemoth from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in just 4.4 seconds, down the quarter mile in 13.2 seconds, and all the way to a top speed electronically limited to 125 mph (200 kph). He specifically asked for the SUV to continue driving like stock, be more powerful and louder, but without waking up the entire neighborhood. So the tuning experts came up with their Stealth Ca setup to make sure the Caddy idles smoothly. A new cold-air induction system, a larger throttle body, a custom supercharger inlet, along with American Racing Headers with high-flow cats, made their way under the hood. The tuners also came up with improved crankcase ventilation and complete ECM and TCM tuning, along with Kong Performance supercharger porting. When they dynoed the Escalade-V, they got over 200 rear-wheel horsepower over the factory rating for a total of 750 rear-wheel horsepower and 650 pound-feet of rear-wheel torque on 93 octane. To make sure he hands over a reliable vehicle back to its owner, Steven Fereday of Late Model Racecraft takes the Escalade-V for a spin and switches to the V-Mode right from the get-go. The V-Mode prepares the SUV for launch. It automatically lowers the air ride suspension by nearly 0.8 inches (20 millimeters). The luxury SUV launches like a rocket and pulls like a freight train, while it handles like stock. The owner is probably waving his warranty goodbye following all the mods under the hood, but it's all in the name of fun and it's surely worth it to him. There is no word on the cost of this build, but a brand-new Escalade-V starts at $168,000 even before the buyer starts to check option boxes. Now, will he hit the drag strip or just drop the kids off at school? Elena started off as a sports reporter and five years later switched to automotive. How does that happen? title: King Harald V death: Tens of thousands mourn as Norway enters a new royal era - AOL.com

Tens of thousands of people gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo on Saturday to pay tribute to Norway's King Harald V, laying flowers and condolence cards a day after the monarch died at the age of 89. A vast display of colourful flowers covered Slottsplassen, the square in front of the palace, as a steady stream of Norwegians filed past. A palace gardener removed several bouquets on the south side of the building to maintain clear pathways, Norwegian broadcaster NRK reported. Palace workers also gathered cards and dried them following an overnight downpour to preserve mourners' messages for posterity, NRK reported. “It’s special, intimate, and lovely. I’m placing my right hand on my chest in gratitude to him and the royal family,” Roni Ervik, 46, told NRK as he paid his respects. He said he was also paying tribute to the late king on behalf of his family, who are from western Norway. Harald V died Friday morning and Crown Prince Haakon, 53, became King Haakon VIII. Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child became Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and the heir to the throne. Haakon knows his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health began to fail in recent years, he stepped in as the country’s regent on several occasions. Later on Saturday, a choir was expected to sing at the Royal Palace Square. The new king was also scheduled to hold audiences with the speaker of Norway’s parliament, the chief justice of the Supreme Court and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway, with Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra also present, NRK reported. Haakon is expected to address the people of Norway in his first speech as new king either later Saturday or in the coming days. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, NRK reported. Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the country’s royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

title: Tonali struggles but Gonzalez impresses - player ratings for Tottenham v Newcastle - BBC
content: Sandro Tonali joined Spurs from Newcastle United in a deal worth up to £100m earleir this summer Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa fired Newcastle United to a 2-0 victory against Tottenham Hotspur. Here's how I rated the players at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and you can see how you scored them below. Antonin Kinsky: Unlike his countryman, Lukas Hornicek, the Spurs goalkeeper had nothing to do in the first half but could only watch on as Elanga's shot went in off the post after the break before Wissa's improvised effort made it 2-0. 5 Archie Gray: Can never fault his effort but is he at his very best at right-back? 5 Micky van de Ven: The captain's first start of the season. Picked up a needless early booking, but went on to make a crucial sliding challenge to deny Wissa inside the box. 6 Jan Paul van Hecke: Got back to make a block to deny Willock. Comfort in possession allowed Spurs to bypass Newcastle press. Went close with header. 6 Andy Robertson: Carried a threat going forward in the first half but could not prevent Dedic winning a header to set up Elanga's goal. 5 Rodrigo Bentancur: Work often goes unseen. Broke up play and won ball back on a number of occasions. 5 Sandro Tonali: A shaky start as he came up against his former club for the first time. Clearly still building up fitness. At fault in build up to both goals. Ironically cheered by away fans as he came off. 4 Mateus Fernandes: First Premier League start for club. Always looked to be positive and deliveries from corners caused one or two problems in first half. 5 Pedro Porro: The World Cup winner played further forward on the right wing and had a couple of openings, seeing a shot blocked by Hall and a dipping volley go just over. 5 Omar Marmoush: Debutant was quickly parachuted into starting line-up, having tormented Newcastle so many times before with Manchester City. Hit side netting on volley. Smart reverse pass created opening for Robertson. 6 Mathys Tel: Saw one stinging effort well-saved, but also frustrated the crowd by giving the ball away. 4 Kudus (on 68, Tel): Welcome return after being sidelined since January with a serious quad injury 5 Subs not used: Dubravka, Senesi, Gallagher, Bergvall, Davies How new signing Gonzalez can be Newcastle's 'Quarterback' Lukas Hornicek: Made saves to keep out Tel, Robertson and van Hecke's efforts when Newcastle were under pressure in the first half. His save from van Hecke's header left head coach Matthias Jaissle clenching his fists on the touchline. 7 Amar Dedic: Another impressive all-round performance from the summer signing little more than a week-and-a-half into his Newcastle career. Great knock-down header to set up first goal. Tino Livramento faces a real battle to win back his place. 7 Malick Thiaw: Captain again in Dan Burn's absence. A proper old-fashioned tussle with Marmoush at times, who kept him on his toes. 6 Sven Botman: Had a shaky pre-season but looking more assured. Appears to be benefitting from a run of games with the same back four. 6 Lewis Hall: Made a huge last-ditch block inside the box to prevent Porro from getting a shot away in first half. Defensively solid and no penalty fears this time. 7 Nico Gonzalez: An impressive debut. Kept composure even after booking. A stunning cross-field ball in the build up to Elanga's goal. 8 Lewis Miley: Goes about his work quietly but keeps the ball so well. 7 Anthony Elanga: Looks a reborn player full of confidence under Jaissle. Scored his second goal in two games with a smart turn and finish in off the post. His was the name repeatedly sung by the away supporters. 7. Joe Willock: Made an instant impact after coming off the bench against Liverpool, but not as effective as a starter on Saturday. Got one of biggest cheers from Newcastle fans for a meaty challenge on Tonali. 5 Harvey Barnes: Fresh from scoring two goals in the midweek win over West Brom in the Carabao Cup, but did not offer same threat this time. Fired one effort way over and failed to pick out a team-mate on one promising breakaway after his cutback went straight into traffic. 5 Yoane Wissa: Led the line in injured William Osula's absence and repeatedly dropped deep to help his side. Clever overhead kick sealed the win. 7 Sean Steur (on 71, Gonzalez): Sent in teasing deliver with corner in build up to Wissa's goal. 7 Nick Woltemade (on 71, Willock): Header set up Newcastle's second from Steur's corner. 7 Subs not used: Jaouen, Schar, Bamba, Toure, Murphy, Ramsey, Shahar After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: Match Report: All Blacks v South Africa, Second Test | Rugby's Greatest Rivalry - All Blacks
content: South African power applied across 80 intense minutes, and a goal-kicking masterclass from wing Cheslin Kolbe, were enough to claim a 33-26 win over the All Blacks at Cape Town, and keep the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series alive. Catch up on all the action, stats and key moments in our Match Centre, After losing the first Test at Ellis Park, the South African response was everything expected, and the All Blacks lacked the assurance they had a week earlier. Kolbe knocked the All Blacks with his four penalty goals, three of them South Africa’s only points of the second half, and three conversions for 18 points, which proved crucial as the All Blacks outscored South Africa in the try count 4-3. The All Blacks enjoyed 57 percent possession while achieving eight line breaks to five and making 154 carries to 104. But those advantages were reduced by determined South African defence. With New Zealand making 246 passes compared to 93 by South Africa, the Springboks had to make 188 tackles, missing 39, compared to 122 tackles by the All Blacks, with 26 misses. In contrast, the All Blacks achieved greater parity at the scrum, claiming 100 per cent of their ball while South Africa managed only 75 per cent. Despite the revived South African spirit, the All Blacks ended the game with a slight chance to secure a draw. Four minutes from time, the All Blacks got within seven points. They again had the benefit of getting wing Will Jordan to space for a run at the corner. He was tackled, but the ball was moved back across the field where flanker and captain Ardie Savea was able to score, with support from replacement lock Patrick Tuipulotu driving him over the line. Into the last minute, replacement lock Lood de Jager was sin-binned for a head-on-head contact on wing Leroy Carter. In the last act of the game, the All Blacks cleared the ball to near halfway for a lineout, and while probing for openings, a key turnover at a tackle on Jordan by replacement Andre Esterhuizen was enough for the Springboks to get the win. Clever use of their bench, with the first substitutions made just before half-time when hooker Malcolm Marx was introduced, helped the Springboks freshen their side at key stages through the second half. By comparison, the All Blacks did not get the same benefits from their changes. South Africa made a storming start, scoring in the first minute after employing the power of their lineout maul to take play deep into the 22m area, and when the ball was released for the backs, centre Jesse Kriel cut through to score. Unsettled, the All Blacks probed for openings at every chance, but it wasn’t until the 15th minute that they were rewarded. From a lineout, the ball was played off the back and moved with both five-eighths Ruben Love and Jordie Barrett using double pumps to draw in the defence before they got the ball to wing Will Jordan, who beat two defenders before passing in to halfback Cam Roigard, who was in support to score. But three minutes later, the penalty issues that afflicted the All Blacks throughout the game were punished when wing Cheslin Kolbe landed the first of his four penalty goals. Then, from the restart, the Springboks got back into the All Blacks' 22m area and built their pressure game again with effect, and it was second five-eighths Damian de Allende who scored. The All Blacks were more settled and built their chances. Again, off a lineout move, No8 Ardie Savea charged onto a ball from Roigard to run into space. The All Blacks worked the ball through the line where and fullback Damian McKenzie used his speed to run in the try. With three points between the sides, it wasn’t until three minutes from half-time that, under penalty pressure, the Springboks extended their lead when, from a lineout play, they worked the ball across the field for skipper and flanker Siya Kolisi to run in the try and secure a 24-14 advantage. That was further extended when Kolbe landed penalty goals in the 48th and 50th minutes. Crossing the 60-minute mark, the All Blacks produced some of their best continuity play; a 14-phase play and a resulting penalty took them close to the line, only for lock Eben Etzebeth to steal the lineout for South Africa to clear. However, a well-taken Springboks box kick was taken by Jordan, who ran ahead to set up the ruck which the All Blacks used to move the ball back across the field, and on the end of the line wing Leroy Carter was given room to wind up his sprint and race his way over for a 65th-minute try. South Africa 33 (Jesse Kriel, Damian de Allende, Siya Kolisi tries; Cheslin Kolbe 3 con, 4pen) New Zealand 26 (Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie, Leroy Carter, Ardie Savea tries; Ruben Love 3 con). title: Norway's King Haakon honors 'dear father' Harald in first speech as sovereign - CNBC
content:
King Haakon VIII of Norway paid homage to his late father as “such a good dad” in his first address to the nation since becoming sovereign, his voice briefly filling with emotion as he evoked his widowed mother, Queen Sonja. King Harald, who emerged from the shadow of his own well-loved, extrovert father to become a reformer during more than three decades on the throne, died on Friday at the age of 89. His son Haakon, dressed in a black suit, white shirt and black tie, praised Harald as a warm family man in a recorded televised speech at the palace. “My dear father, thank you for being such a good dad for Martha and I,” he said, referring to his sister, Princess Martha Louise. “I am going to miss him. I am going to miss his laughter. I am going to miss his good-natured way to meet people and situations,” he continued, sitting behind a desk, with a portrait of a smiling Harald to his left. He noted that Saturday should have been the celebration of the 58th wedding anniversary of Harald and Queen Sonja, who survives him. “Congratulations on your wedding anniversary, dear Mummy,” Haakon said, his voice appearing briefly overtaken by emotion. Haakon stressed he would do things his own way, as his father did before him, and reiterated the foundations of Norway as a constitutional monarchy, embodied by the oath he will take in parliament on Tuesday to protect the country’s constitution and laws. “We believe in our system of self-governance — and in democracy. We believe in a society built on the rule of law — where every individual has equal worth,” he said. Haakon automatically became king upon his father’s death under Norway’s constitutional monarchy. There will be no coronation as they were abolished by parliament in 1908. “We believe in a Norway where there is room for everyone. We shall feel the strength of our community - and know deep within ourselves that we are one people,” he said. At the end of his speech, outside the palace, mourners who had been watching on their mobile phones broke into spontaneous applause. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere, speaking to Reuters minutes before the broadcast of the speech, said Haakon shared many qualities with his father. “This King has something from his father, which is the ability to create an atmosphere of togetherness,” he said in an interview outside the palace. Since Harald’s passing, people have streamed in their tens of thousands to say goodbye to the late king at the royal palace, where he lies in state, with many well-wishers remembering his sense of inclusiveness and tolerance. Flags were flying at half-mast throughout the country and portraits of the late king in gala uniform could be seen at bus stops, trams and metro stations to shops, offices and public buildings. The main avenue in central Oslo, Karl Johan, was tightly packed with people from all walks of life heading towards the palace, clutching flowers, handwritten cards, drawings and small national flags. Mourners praised the late king’s spirit of inclusiveness. “He meant a lot to us immigrants ... We felt really very included. So, thanks to him, I feel so Norwegian,” Veselina Vitanova, a 43-year-old teacher originally from Bulgaria, told Reuters outside the palace. Another referred to a speech Harald delivered in 2016 that went viral worldwide, in which he said: “Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys and girls and boys who love each other”. “It embodies the way he felt about people and the way he wanted us Norwegians to feel about each other,” said Mari Eidsvaag, 32, who wore a T-shirt emblazoned with that sentence, a rainbow and a drawing of King Harald. “I think it’s a very important statement, especially these days,” she told Reuters. title: Sony a7R V vs a7 V vs a7R VI: 2026 - Fstoppers
content: Choosing a Sony body in the $3,000 to $5,000 range means weighing resolution, speed, and battery life against a price that keeps shifting on the used market. The a7R V, a7 V, and a7R VI look nearly identical in the hand, yet they behave very differently once you start shooting. Having bought all three with his own money, Luca Petralia walks through the physical differences, the stills performance, and the video capabilities before landing on a recommendation tied to your budget and your work. He points out small things first, like the a7R VI's dedicated button-illumination control and its reworked mode dial with an asterisk position that stores ten extra custom setups per shooting scenario. Storage separates the tiers, too. Both the a7R V and a7R VI carry dual hybrid slots that take CFexpress Type A or SD, while the a7 V drops to one hybrid slot and one SD slot. Petralia thinks a $3,000 camera should have matched the others there, though he stops short of calling it a deal breaker. Battery life is where the a7R VI pulls ahead in a way that surprised even Petralia. The a7R V and a7 V share the older NP-FZ100 battery, while the a7R VI uses Sony's newer NP-FW100. In a week of shooting nearly 1,800 frames in a single session, he still had 40 percent left, and he simply couldn't drain it in one outing. That new battery costs more, third-party versions won't appear for a while, and it makes the body slightly larger, which meant his existing cage no longer fit. The stacked-sensor architecture drives the bigger gains: the a7R V uses a conventional CMOS sensor, the a7 V a partially stacked sensor, and the a7R VI a fully stacked one. That difference makes the electronic shutter genuinely usable on the two newer bodies, unlocking 30 frames per second at full bit depth with a blackout-free viewfinder. If you shoot in dim rooms or after dark, the dual base ISO on the a7 V and a7R VI is the spec that quietly reshapes your workflow. A single base ISO sensor is cleanest at one sensitivity, but a dual base sensor gives you a second point where the signal-to-noise ratio resets. The a7 V's second base sits at ISO 8,000 and the a7R VI's at ISO 5,000, both alongside a base of 800. That means when a scene pushes you toward ISO 3,200, you're often better off jumping to the higher base and pulling exposure back with an ND filter, shutter, or aperture, because the file comes out cleaner despite the higher number on the dial. It runs against the instinct to keep ISO as low as possible, and it's a habit worth building if either of these bodies ends up in your bag. The same thinking has spread across Sony's lineup and into rival cameras from Panasonic and Nikon, so learning to read dual base ISO now pays off well beyond these three. On video, Petralia is candid that he ran his channel on the a7R V for a year and a half without trouble. The newer sensors still change the math. The a7R V caps 4K 60p with a heavy crop, while the a7 V delivers 4K 60p with no crop using angle-of-view priority, and 4K 120p in Super 35. The a7R VI adds only a very small crop at 4K 120. Oversampling differs as well, with the a7 V pulling 4K from 7K, the a7R VI from 5K, and the a7R V using line skipping. He's clear that you won't spot line skipping in normal viewing unless you pixel-peep side by side. His verdict splits along budget and intent, and it's worth hearing him lay out exactly who each camera suits, including why a used a7R V near $2,000 to $2,500 might be the sharpest value of the three and which body he's keeping versus selling. title: Tens of thousands mourn King Harald V in Oslo as Norway enters a new royal era - WANE 15
content: Presiding Bishop of the Church of Norway Olav Fykse Tveit lays flowers at the Palace Square to pay respects to Norway's King Harald V, a day after he died at 89, in Oslo, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Amanda Pedersen Giske/NTB Scanpix via AP) OSLO, Norway (AP) — King Haakon VIII of Norway used his first speech in his new role to eulogize his father, King Harald V, as a loving parent and dedicated monarch a day after he died at 89. “We are in mourning. At the same time, it brings us comfort and strength to know that so many are mourning with us,” the king said wearing a black suit as his speech was shown live on public television. After Harald V’s death on Friday morning, the crown prince became King Haakon VIII immediately. He thanked the people for their outpouring of compassion and remembered what a loving father and husband Harald had been. Tens of thousands of mourners paid their respects, placing flowers and condolence cards outside the royal palace in Oslo, where the coffin arrived late Friday from the hospital. Across the country, churches and city halls opened specially so people could light candles, and write their thoughts about the deceased king in condolence books. “It has been a powerful and moving experience to see the Palace Square filled with people, flowers, messages of condolence, and candles. Thank you so much,” 53-year-old Haakon said, sitting on a wooden desk next to his father’s portrait and two white candles. “As king, my father represented Norway and the Norwegian people with pride and joy, through visits around the country, at events here at the royal palace, and while working on Norway’s behalf around the world,” Haakon said. “I’m going to miss him. I’ll miss his laughter. His good-natured way of dealing with people and situations,” he added, trying to hold back his tears as he vowed to give everything for the country in the future as its new king. “And that means — in the ultimate sense — being willing to risk everything, even one’s life, for Norway’s freedom and independence.” Haakon adopted the motto “All for Norway,” which dates back to his great-grandfather. His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child, Ingrid Alexandra, became crown princess and heir to the throne. Earlier on Saturday, the new king and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra welcomed Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and the presiding bishop of the Lutheran Church of Norway to the palace where King Harald’s coffin was lying in state, the royal palace said in a statement. On Sunday morning, the Church of Norway is holding memorial services across the country, with the royal family expected to attend the service at Asker Church, southwest of Oslo, the palace said. Haakon is well acquainted with his royal obligations. As his father aged and his health declined in recent years, Haakon stepped in as regent on several occasions. His tasks in the near future will include shoring up support for the monarchy following controversies over his wife’s past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson’s rape conviction. A date for the funeral has not been set, but the country is officially in a state of mourning and some people decided to postpone celebrations such as weddings and baptisms until after the mourning period has passed, Norwegian public broadcaster NRK reported. Norway’s monarchy has old roots, tracing its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. Today, the role is largely symbolic as power lies with an elected parliament, but the royal family retains celebrity and a role in promoting the wealthy nation around the world.

title: Leeds v Brentford: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: Elland Road will be abuzz with anticipation as Leeds United host Brentford on Sunday (14:00 BST) in a showdown between two sides that have had excellent starts to the new campaign. Leeds won their opening two fixtures – both at Nottingham Forest, in the Premier League (1-0) and then the Carabao Cup (2-0) – adding further momentum to some summer transfers that have got pulses racing in West Yorkshire. Brentford also have two wins from two, albeit they have earned their victories in more spectacular style. They smashed Tottenham 3-0 in their Premier League opener before running riot at Birmingham City in the EFL Cup to win 6-1. Last season, both Leeds and Brentford enjoyed fine campaigns, with their physical play vital to their success. So unsurprisingly, in the opening weekend of the season, the two teams to win the most duels were Leeds with 66 and Brentford with 62. Although Brentford, in ninth, finished ahead of Leeds, who were 14th, last term, since December there has not been much between the two teams at all. Since the start of December 2025, only five teams have won more points in the Premier League than the 39 accrued by Leeds United, while only three sides have won more points on home soil than the Whites in that time, with 24. Brentford have amassed a total of 37 points in the same time frame. After two away games to start the season, there will be an eagerness among the Leeds fans to get their campaign up and running on home soil, especially with some new faces among a bolstered squad. New goalkeeper James Trafford, who arrived in a £45m transfer from Manchester City, has impressed with two clean sheets. He has made five saves across his first two matches, while Bosnia defender Tarik Muharemovic, a £34m arrival from Sassuolo, has also won supporters over quickly. Harry Wilson also made the move to Leeds this summer, and he won't mind the sight of Brentford's red and white stripes on Sunday. There is no club he has scored against more often than the Bees, with four goals in the Premier League. Even if Wilson were to net, Brentford would still fancy their chances of outgunning Leeds given their start to the campaign. Keith Andrews' side should have won by more in their 3-0 victory over Spurs – Igor Thiago missed a penalty in that encounter – while against Birmingham, their Premier League class was clear as they rattled in six. In what have been two very different types of tests so far, Brentford have been completely dominant. The positive intent throughout the side was summed up by the fact that seven players had shots against Spurs. They also compiled an xG of 3.96 on the day, their most in a Premier League game since January 2025 against Southampton. The win also allowed Brentford to show off their multidimensional attacking threat. In the build-up to their first goal, the Bees put together 15 passes, while they also had more shots from set pieces, with 14, than any other team in the division.

title: Anne V: Beyond the Label. - theperfectmagazine.com
content: By using this website, you agree to our use of cookies. We use cookies to provide you with a great experience and to help our website run effectively. I met Anne V the way only fashion can introduce two people. We first crossed paths in Biarritz at an exhibition hosted by art dealer Lucy Chadwick before a cruise show in April. Then again with Katie Grand on Rue Cambon. We stayed in touch. By haute couture three months later, Anne and  I were meeting for coffee at 9.45am so we could be first in line when the flagship opened. Early bird special! Minutes later, we were sharing a dressing room, half naked, trying on the same pair of jeans  and the same shearling bomber jacket.  We both bought them. Fashion has always had an addiction to labels. Anne Vyalitsyna’s greatest act of defiance was refusing to accept one. Born in Russia, Anne landed her breakthrough at 15 with the Chanel Chance campaign by Jean-Paul Goude. It came down to Anne and another young Ukrainian model, Diana Kandyba, sharing a tiny Paris hotel room while competing for the same job. ‘I got it, and she didn’t,’ Anne says. ‘I had to go back and sleep beside her. She was so happy for me. I will never forget that.’ ‘What’s yours will find you,’ Anne says. ‘What’s not yours will leave you. It taught me never to be jealous. We need to make the pie bigger, not smaller.’ From then on, Anne found herself confronting fashion’s need to categorise. Editorial or commercial. Vogue or Sports Illustrated. Prada or Victoria’s Secret. ‘I never understood why I couldn’t  be a super high-fashion girl with no eyebrows and a major red lip, then go  and do Victoria’s Secret,’ she says.  ‘I give everything when I do one, and I give everything when I do the other. Why can’t I do both?’ The gatekeepers had already made up their minds. Boxes are easier to sell than women. Because fashion has always preferred archetypes to people. ‘Being versatile backfired on me a lot,’ she says. ‘I probably could have done more major shit if I had stayed exclusively in high fashion. It was really hard for high-fashion people to accept me at a size four or six. I was doing more commercial things when I was heavier.’ While others saw a changing body, Katie Grand saw the same model. At Love, at Giles, at Marc Jacobs and at the Louis Vuitton shows she styled, she continued to back Anne. ‘Katie has always loved a woman,’ Anne says. ‘She loved me at every size and shape. I always felt there was one person who sees me.’ ‘My thirties were really fucking hard,’ Anne says. ‘People see you doing well, but they don’t always want to hear about the hard years. I was scared to turn 40 – not because I was afraid of getting older, but because I was terrified that the same energy would continue into another decade. When you’re 20 and have no money, you can sleep on your friend’s couch. At 40, with your mother and child living with you, you are not going to fucking do that.’ Anne says those difficult years taught her something fashion rarely rewards: staying in the moment. ‘I was always lucky and grateful,’ she says. ‘But when I was younger, it was difficult to stay in the moment. You completed something enormous and immediately asked, what’s next?’ Now, she says, ‘I’m having an amazing period in my life, and I’m trying to be inside it. Not rushing past it. Not asking what’s next. Just saying thank you.’ After years of being ‘incredibly frugal’, Anne bought the jacket she wore in Matthieu Blazy’s first Métiers d’Art show for her daughter to inherit. ‘Now I look back and think, holy shit, if this moment in my career had happened a few years earlier, I wouldn’t have been able to handle it. I’m grateful I had that time with my daughter. I want her to understand: this is why I do what I do. This is why I fell in love with modelling and fashion.’ She wants her daughter to one day say, ‘This is the jacket my mom wore. I was there at the fitting. I met Matthieu. I saw her wear it. And now my mom owns that jacket.’ That morning in July on Rue Cambon, we bought the same jacket. Mine was for now. Anne was already imagining who would wear hers next.

content: South Africa will look to hit back in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series after New Zealand went 1-0 up with victory at Ellis Park. A tremendous performance from the All Blacks saw them turn over their hosts 33-16 in the first Test, and another win here would ensure that Dave Rennie's side cannot be beaten in this four-match series. title: Interstellar Travel V: Warp Drives, Wormholes, and Halo Drives - Universe Today
content:
Welcome back to our series on Interstellar Travel, where we look at the many proposals made for sending missions to the stars since the dawn of the Space Age. In our first installment, we examined how Cold War-era developments in nuclear weapons and rockets paralleled advances in space exploration, resulting in proposals for nuclear rockets. We then examined how the creation of thermonuclear weapons led to applications in fusion propulsion. Then we looked at how the discovery and creation of positrons and anti-protons fueled proposals for spacecraft driven by antimatter propulsion. In our fourth installment, we addressed the most practical options for sending missions to interstellar space, including solar sails, magnetic sails, and directed-energy propulsion (DEP). In our fifth installment, we'll examine the most exotic proposals ever made that could (in theory) enable interstellar spaceflight someday. As we explored in a previous article, a ship relying on conventional propulsion methods would take thousands of years. And while theoretical methods exist that could shorten transits to a few decades, they would be very expensive to build and require tremendous amounts of propellant. Alas, there are always those long-shot proposals, the kind that straddle the line between science fiction and fact, that still give us hope. Among them are the warp drive, wormhole travel, and using black holes to achieve velocities approaching the speed of light. This artist’s impression shows the planet Proxima b orbiting the red dwarf star Proxima Centauri, the closest star to our Solar System. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser. As noted in our inaugural installment, there is no shortage of planets beyond the Solar System (exoplanets) that are well worth exploring. To date, scientists have confirmed the existence of 6,354 exoplanets in 4,756 star systems. In fact, that number has increased since this series began on July 31st! At that time, the census was 6,333 confirmed exoplanets in 4,747 systems. Doing the math, that means that 21 more exoplanets in 9 star systems have been confirmed in less than a month. What's more, while "Earth-like" (rocky) planets are rare, with the total still at 222 confirmations, they are surprisingly abundant in our stellar neighborhood. In fact, within 50 light-years of Earth, there are 31 known terrestrial planets, 30 of which orbit low-mass, M-type red dwarf stars. The closest of these is Proxima b, a rocky planet orbiting Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf star 4.25 light-years from Earth. Discovered in 2016, the planet has an estimated surface temperature of -39 °C (-38 °F), compared to 15 °C (59 °F) for Earth. While scientists are divided on whether this planet is habitable, there are scenarios in which Proxima b could support life. Regardless, Proxima b's proximity to Earth makes it the natural choice for an interstellar mission and likely the first stop in humanity's exploration beyond the Solar System (should that ever occur). So what can the most exotic propulsion methods ever devised do to get us there? Fans of science fiction are certainly familiar with the concept of the Warp Drive. While the idea has existed for decades, it has largely been confined to the realm of science fiction and pure speculation. It was not until 1994 that an actual proposal was made for how a warp drive could work within the realm of known physics. This proposal is credited to Mexican theoretical physicist Miguel Alcubierre, who proposed what would become known as the "Alcubierre Drive" as part of his Ph.D. studies at Cardiff University, Wales. Alcubierre described the concept in a 1994 paper titled "The warp drive: hyper-fast travel within general relativity," in which he argued that it was possible to move faster than the speed of light (FTL) without violating Einstein's Theory of Relativity. More specifically, he distinguished between Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity (SR) and his General Theory of Relativity (GR). Annotated graphic of a spacecraft within a warp bubble, showing the 1) vertical dimension (expanding spacetime), 2) interior of the warp bubble, and 3) negative dimension (contracting spacetime). Credit: Kris Holland/Matt Jeffries "When we study special relativity, we learn that nothing can travel faster than the speed of light," he wrote. "This fact is still true in general relativity, though in this case one must be somewhat more precise: in general relativity, nothing can travel locally faster than the speed of light." The concept involves stretching the fabric of space-time in a wave (a "warp bubble"), which would theoretically cause the space ahead of it to contract and the space behind it to expand. An object inside this wave could then ride it to super-relativistic speeds. As he explained it: The basic idea can be more easily understood if we think for a moment in the inflationary phase of the early Universe, and consider the relative speed of separation of two comoving observers. It is easy to convince oneself that, if we define this relative speed as the rate of change of proper spatial distance over proper time, we will obtain a value that is much larger than the speed of light. This doesn’t mean that our observers will be traveling faster than light: they always move inside their local light-cones. The enormous speed of separation comes from the expansion of spacetime itself. Since the ship is being carried along as it moves (but is not moving itself), the rules of spacetime and GR would cease to apply since this method does not rely on moving faster than light in the local sense. It is only FTL in the sense that a ship inside the bubble would reach another star before a beamed transmission traveled the same distance. The theoretical basis of this drive system, where Alcubierre proposed resolutions to Einstein's field equations for GR, is known as the Alcubierre Metric. As Alcubierre argued, quantum field theory allows for regions of spacetime with negative energy densities to exist. This is known as the Casimir Effect, the attractive force between two surfaces in a vacuum. If a "ring" of negative mass could be created around a spacecraft, spacetime could theoretically contract in front of the ship and expand behind it. As he wrote: By a purely local expansion of spacetime behind the spaceship and an opposite contraction in front of it, motion faster than the speed of light as seen by observers outside the disturbed region is possible. The resulting distortion is reminiscent of the "warp drive" of science fiction. However, just as it happens with wormholes, exotic matter will be needed in order to generate a distortion of spacetime. However, the concept has its share of theoretical challenges. According to Alcubierre's original paper, the amount of negative mass (or "exotic matter") required to achieve a warp field was beyond anything humanity could achieve. There are also many uncertainties, including violations of causality, the effect on spacetime at the destination, and whether such a system would be safe for those riding the wave. In addition, all proposed warp-drive theories violate various energy conditions. In the past fifteen years, the Alcubierre Drive has received renewed attention, thanks in large part to NASA scientist Harold "Sonny" White. Dr. White's involvement began in 2011 while preparing to deliver a speech at the first 100 Year Starship symposium, a joint project hosted by NASA and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). White chose to discuss Alcubierre's field equations, during which time he made some calculations and found that the energy requirements may actually be within the realm of possibility. In 2012, White announced that he and his colleagues at the Advanced Propulsion Physics Research Laboratory (NASA Eagleworks) had begun researching the concept. In a paper titled "Warp Field Mechanics 101," White described how his team had built an interferometer for detecting spatial distortions produced by the expanding and contracting spacetime of the Alcubierre Metric. In 2013, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory published results of a warp field test conducted under vacuum conditions, which were reported as "inconclusive." By 2019, NASA effectively ended its warp drive and advanced propulsion research after White left the agency. A year later, White began working with engineers and scientists at the Limitless Space Institute (LSI), a non-profit organization dedicated to education, outreach, and advanced propulsion methods, with the ultimate purpose of creating the first warp drive! White's research builds on the work of his colleague, astrophysicist Richard Obousy, who co-founded Project Icarus with starship engineer Kevin Long in 2009. Also in 2009, Obousy and co-author Aram Saharian released a study titled "Casimir energy and the possibility of higher dimensional manipulation," which considered how next-generation particle accelerators could produce fields that alter the density of dark energy locally, changing the expansion of spacetime. Their calculations also indicated that this could be done with a negative mass about the size of Jupiter (1.898 x 1024 kg; 4.18 x 1024 lbs). While their calculations indicated that it was mathematically possible to generate a warp bubble, the energy requirement is beyond anything humanity can currently conceive. But as White explained to Universe Today in a previous interview, he and his fellow researchers showed how reconsidering the "shell-thickness parameter" of the warp bubble could further reduce the energy requirement. In short, a thicker warp shell would reduce the strain on spacetime, thus allowing a spacecraft to achieve speeds of up to 10 times the speed of light (10 c) using only two metric tons (2.2 U.S. tons) of exotic matter. Alas, while the concept has become much more feasible in recent years, it is still a theoretical proposal. At present, scientists have not confirmed the existence of negative mass, and a proof of concept is still a long way off. Here's another staple of science fiction, one which fans are sure to recognize. To break it down, wormholes are theoretical tunnels that connect two points in spacetime. The theory emerged in the early 20th century in response to Einstein's General Theory of Relativity, which established that the speed of light could not be reached or exceeded. 
The first to postulate their existence was German physicist and astronomer Karl Schwarzschild, whose solutions to Einstein's field equation (the Schwarzschild metric) provided the first theoretical basis for black holes. A consequence of the Schwarzschild metric is what he termed "eternal black holes," which were essentially connections between different points in spacetime. Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen similarly postulated the existence of wormholes, known as Einstein-Rosen Bridges, in a 1935 paper titled “The Particle Problem in the General Theory of Relativity.” According to their paper, this bridge would connect a regular black hole (from which nothing can escape) and a "white hole" (from which nothing can enter). Unfortunately, the "bridge" is located behind the black hole's event horizon, so any spacecraft entering the black hole would be crushed into the singularity. What's more, the Schwarzschild Metric showed wormholes to be unstable, as they would collapse too quickly for anything to cross from one end to the other. For a wormhole to be stable (a traversable wormhole), it requires negative mass. While negative mass is yet to be discovered, negative energy exists in many quantum scenarios (again, the Casimir Effect), In a series of papers, Prof. Juan Maldacena from the Institute for Advanced Study and Alexey Milekhin, a graduate student at Princeton University, explored the possibility of humans traversing wormholes. In the first, "Traversable wormholes in four dimensions," they proposed how charged massless fermions could give rise to a Casimir-like energy, supporting a stable wormhole. In their second paper, "Humanly traversable wormholes,," they argued that these wormholes were consistent with the Standard Model of Particle Physics. However, they found this scenario would apply only to microscopic black holes, since the entire process is in the quantum realm. To be traversable by humans, wormholes would need to be significantly larger, requiring physics that go beyond the Standard Model. To that end, they adopted the Randall-Sundrum II model (aka. 5-dimensional warped geometry theory), from which they derived intermediately-sized charged black holes. But these would generate powerful tidal forces, so a spacecraft would need a significant boost factor to bypass them and enter the wormhole. Meanwhile, research on Einstein-Rosen Bridges by Daniel Jafferis of Harvard University showed that while possible, stable wormholes would take longer to traverse than normal space. From the traveler's perspective, virtually no time would have passed but the travel time would seem much longer to an outsider. This is consistent with General Relativity and the time dilation caused by relativistic travel. Once again, though, the issue comes down to negative mass, which is required in all cases to keep wormholes stable. Since scientists have no idea how to generate negative mass, or find it as a natural by-product of cosmic processes, wormhole travel remains the stuff of theory and science fiction. To recap, traveling to even the nearest stars beyond our Solar System is always subject to the tyranny of General Relativity. To reach a significant velocity and get there in a human's lifetime, an incredible amount of energy is required. This means a tremendous amount of propellant, tiny spacecraft, massive laser arrays, exotic physics, or a combination of these. But what if it was possible to accelerate a spacecraft to relativistic speeds without the need for propellant? This is the logic of the Halo Drive, a concept proposed by Prof. David Kipping of Columbia University and the leader of its Cool Worlds lab. Prof. Kipping described this concept in a 2019 paper, where he addressed these challenges and devised a rather exotic solution. To this, Kipping suggests a modified version of what is known as the "Dyson Slingshot," an idea proposed by venerated theoretical physicist Freeman Dyson (inventor of the Dyson Sphere). In the 1963 anthology Interstellar Communications (Chapter 12: "Gravitational Machines"), Dyson described how spacecraft could slingshot around compact binary stars to gain a significant boost in velocity. As Dyson described it, a ship would be sent to a compact binary system where it would perform a gravity-assist maneuver with the two stars. The spacecraft would pick up speed from the stars' intense gravity, adding the equivalent of twice their rotational velocity to its own, before being flung out of the system. Expanding on this, Kipping proposed that the same gravity-assist maneuver could be accomplished using a rapidly rotating black hole. This idea calls to mind the Penrose Process, proposed by English mathematical physicist and Nobel-prize winner Roger Penrose. In 1971, Penrose proposed that energy could be extracted from a black hole's ergosphere, the region just outside the event horizon. In this region, infalling matter is accelerated to velocities approaching the speed of light, emitting tremendous energy in the process. By harnessing the multi-wavelength radiation emitted by the infalling matter, an intelligent species would have a virtually inexhaustible supply of energy. In the case of the Halo Drive, however, a spacecraft would insert itself into the ergosphere, allowing the black hole's rapid rotation to accelerate it to near-to-light (NTL) velocities. And just like Dyson's gravitational machines, the spacecraft would break off from the ergosphere and travel towards its destination at incredible speeds. This power of gravitational slingshots is supported by the relatively recent discovery of hyper-velocity stars. According to research from the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA), these stars are a result of galactic mergers and interaction with massive black holes, which causes them to be kicked out of their galaxies at speeds of ~30,000 to 100,000 km/s (18,600 to 62,000 mps) - one-tenth to one-third the speed of light. But of course, the Halo Drive presents numerous challenges and some notable disadvantages. In addition to requiring a spacecraft capable of withstanding intense radiation, it would also need to be strong enough structurally to handle the stresses of the intense acceleration it imparts. The process also demands tremendous precision; otherwise, the ship and crew could be pulled apart in the black hole's maw. On top of that, there's the matter of reaching the black hole, which would require significant propellant and long transit times. Ultimately, the most exotic concepts for achieving interstellar travel suffer from the same problems as many of the less exotic ones. In short, they require tremendous amounts of energy, significant advances in science, and/or the discovery of exotic physics and matter. At the same time, these concepts remain fixed in the popular imagination and continue to be the subject of research because they instill hope. With the right scientific breakthrough and commitment, an FTL or NTL concept could be realized that would deliver us to distant worlds. The kind of hope that says "someday this will be possible" is always a welcome relief whenever we're faced with the harsh realities of spaceflight and the sheer grandeur of the Universe. Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

title: King Harald V of Norway Has Died After 35 Years On the Throne. Meet His Successor, Haakon - Time Magazine
content: This website uses cookies to enhance user experience and to analyze performance and traffic on our website. We also share information about your use of our site with our social media, advertising and analytics partners. Follow this section to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. Follow this tag to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. The new King and Queen of Norway, Mette-Marit and Haakon, are seen here at the Norwegian Constitution Day in Oslo on May 17, 2026. Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts. King Harald V of Norway, a reformer and Europe’s oldest monarch, died Friday at the age of 89. His son, the newly-proclaimed King Haakon VIII, has inherited the Norwegian throne. Harald passed away peacefully in his sleep at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet at 6:35 a.m., local time, the Royal Palace of Norway said. “A whole nation is in mourning and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway,” said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. “For more than three decades as monarch, Harald V demonstrated an unwavering faith in the Norwegian people. He helped us to see the best in ourselves—and in one another.” Harald had been admitted to the hospital on Aug. 17 and placed on sick leave after corticosteroid treatment for haemolytic anemia caused fluid retention that required hospital care, the palace revealed. His son, then-Crown Prince Haakon, 53, served as regent while his father was on leave. In an update on Aug. 23, the palace announced the King’s condition had worsened and that he would remain in the hospital to receive antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream. In recent days, Norwegians had begun to lay flowers in front of the palace in Oslo after the royal household said his condition had become “very serious.” Harald has been described as a monarch who modernized the institution. His marriage broke with royal convention when he wed the non-royal Sonja Haraldsen in 1968 after a lengthy struggle for permission from his family. In a widely noted 2016 Palace garden speech, Harald defined Norwegianness as encompassing immigrants, people of different religions, and members of the LGBTQ+ community. While Norway is a constitutional monarchy, with the king serving as head of state similar to other royal houses in Europe, Norwegian monarchs have largely held symbolic roles, as legislative power rests with an elected parliament. Stortinget, Norway’s parliament, said Friday that the King’s reign “was marked by closeness to the people” thanks to “the unifying way in which he has exercised his royal duties.” Norway will observe a period of mourning, with flags at royal residences, government buildings, and military installations set to remain at half-mast. Church bells rang out on Friday and thousands of people lined the streets as Harald V's coffin, accompanied by a motorcade of black cars, was transported to the Royal Palace in Oslo. As Norway mourns its long-reigning monarch, thoughts are also turning to his successor, who has been tasked with carrying on his father's legacy. Here’s what to know about what comes next and how King Harald is being remembered by his peers and European leaders. When a monarch in Norway passes away, the next person in the order of succession automatically becomes King or Queen, as the country cannot be without a head of state. While succession was previously restricted to male heirs, since 1990 the Constitution was amended so female and male children would be included on an equal footing in the order of succession. However, for those born before the change, a male child retains precedence over an older female sibling. As such, although Princess Märtha Louise was Harald’s eldest child, the crown automatically passed down to his son, Haakon. King Haakon VIII’s wife, Mette-Marit Tjessem Høiby, is the new Queen of Norway. The late King Harald's wife, Queen Sonja, will also retain her title. Haakon and Mette-Marit's daughter Ingrid Alexandra is now Crown Princess and heir apparent—the next person in line to the throne. The Norwegian government convened for an extraordinary cabinet meeting at the palace on Friday at 11:30 a.m., local time, where ministers met the new King. Haakon announced his royal motto, opting to keep the words used by his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather: "All for Norway." There will be no formal coronation for Haakon as Norway’s parliament removed the constitutional requirement for coronations in 1908, deeming the ceremony to be undemocratic and outdated. As the only son of Harald and Sonja, Haakon somewhat broke with tradition in his younger years when he moved out of the country to attend the University of California, Berkeley, where he obtained a BA in political science in 1999. Haakon wed Mette-Marit in 2001, a non-royal and single mother of Marius Borg Høiby. The couple welcomed their first child together, Ingrid Alexandra, in 2004 and had their son, Sverre Magnus, a year later. Marius Borg Høiby, Mette-Marit’s eldest child, was found guilty of two counts of rape and was sentenced to four years in prison in June. In recent years, Mette-Marit has suffered with poor health, after being diagnosed with a chronic lung disease—what the palace referred to as an “unusual variant of fibrosis”—in 2018. In July, Mette-Marit shared a statement upon being discharged from hospital after undergoing a lung transplant. “It has given me the gift of life, and words fall short when I try to describe how grateful and humble I am for this,” she said of the surgery. Mette-Marit has come under scrutiny over her contact with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Files released by the Justice Department in January showed she had maintained correspondence with Epstein in the years after he pled guilty on two counts of soliciting prostitution from a minor in 2008. “Jeffrey Epstein is personally responsible for his actions. I must take responsibility for not checking Epstein’s background more thoroughly and for not understanding quickly enough what kind of person he was,” Mette-Marit said in a statement on Jan. 30 2026. “I deeply regret that, and this is a responsibility I must take. I showed poor judgment and regret ever having had any contact with Epstein. It is simply embarrassing. I want to express my deep sympathy and solidarity with the victims of the abuses committed by Jeffrey Epstein.” During a TV interview in March, Mette-Marit, while sitting beside her husband Haakon, said she wished she had never met Epstein and again expressed regret over the contact. Her Majesty Queen Sonja of Norway and His Majesty King Harald of Norway attend a Norwegian Constitution Day event at the Royal Palace in Oslo, Norway, on May 17, 2026. Ole Hagen––Getty Images Tributes have poured in from around the world to honor the late King and his legacy. Britain’s King Charles III, who is a cousin of Harald, said he and his wife, Queen Camilla, had learned of the news with “the most profound sadness.” “For thirty-five years, King Harald served his people with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility,” Charles said. “As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades.” Spain’s monarchy said Harald was “an example of responsibility, dignity, simplicity, and tireless dedication to the service of Norway and its people, before and during his 35 years of reign.” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte described the late King as a “dedicated leader,” whose “military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO.” Harald's military roots go back to when he attended the Norwegian Military Academy in Oslo as a young royal and went on to be appointed general and admiral in 1977, as part of the royal tradition where the Crown Prince is appointed to the highest rank in the branches of defense at the age of 40. Senior officials within the European Union also offered their condolences, with Norway serving as a close trading and security partner of the bloc. E.U. foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Harald was “truly the people’s King, a lifelong defender of freedom and champion of an open Norwegian democracy and society.” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the late King had brought Norwegians together “in moments of joy and sorrow.” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz lamented that Norway had lost “a great personality who stood for composure and unity,” while French President Emmanuel Macron said Harald had “worked tirelessly throughout his reign to strengthen the bonds uniting Norway and France.” Norwegian soccer player Erling Haaland, who met with the late King in July after returning from the World Cup 2026, said: “Rest in peace, King Harald. Thank you for everything you meant to Norway. It was an honor to meet you." © 2026 TIME USA, LLC. All Rights Reserved.
